item.title: Ultrafast Optical Probing of Laser Processing
item.description: arXiv:2509.03220v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Laser treatment has emerged into a cornerstone of industrial manufacturing. This creates the demand to understand in detail the involved physical processes and their dynamics, to control the process, and to keep guard in-situ the laser manufacturing steps. Given the contactless interaction of light with matter, particularly optical methods appear most suitable for probing laser processing. This chapter reviews the current scientific and technological state of analyzing laser-based material processing by short and ultrashort optical pulses. For that, sequential passive interrogation of material properties (via reflection, absorption, scattering, diffraction, interference, or specific nonlinear responses) can be employed through so-called pump-probe techniques (where the time-resolution is not given by the detector response time but by the duration of an electromagnetic probe pulse that is interrogating the transient scenery at a controlled delay (typ. fs to \mu s) with respect to the arrival of the pump laser pulse). These approaches are capable to analyze on microscopic to macroscopic scales a plethora of different processes involved in laser processing, such as heating, melting, ablation, plasma- and shockwave-formation, optical breakdown in surrounding liquids and gases, shielding and accumulation effects, surface solidification and restructuring, etc. A special focus is set on the variety of ultrafast optical imaging schemes for visualizing the dynamics of laser processing at the surface and in the bulk of the irradiated materials, including photography and microscopy, holography, tomography, ptychography, and coherent diffractive imaging. The chapter provides a historic survey, highlights important scientific and technological developments and breakthroughs, discusses selected applications, explores the requirements and current limitations, and sheds light on emerging future trends.
item.dc:creator: J\"orn Bonse

item.title: How Does Incubation Affect Laser Material Processing?
item.description: arXiv:2509.08326v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In the last decades, the subject of laser-induced damage (LID) moved from a topic of scientific interest toward laser material processing for technical applications. When using pulsed lasers, the cumulative effect known as incubation is one of the most fundamental features of the processing event. Incubation manifests by the fact that the critical fluence for LID (known as laser-induced damage threshold, LIDT) depends on the number of pulses N exciting one spot on the sample. In most cases, the threshold fluence decreases with N starting from the single-shot ablation threshold and remains constant for large N. No ablation or damage occurs for any N, if the fluence is kept below the multiple-pulse threshold. In contrast, examples where the LIDT increases with N have been reported. The latter effect is known as laser conditioning and is advantageously used when ramping up the power of high-power laser systems. Incubation has been described for many types of solids; the motivation for these comprehensive efforts is twofold. Firstly, one tries to prevent the damage of optical materials in the beam path of high-energy or high-peak-power lasers. Secondly, one deliberately uses this damage for the sculpting of components. In this chapter, we introduce the reader to the mechanisms of incubation. We are going to look at the parameters controlling LID and highlight the peculiarity of the parameter "number of pulses". We will give an overview of the experimental work done in a variety of materials. There are several physical and chemical mechanisms proposed that govern incubation, and there are several mathematical models to describe the behavior of threshold fluence and ablation rate in dependence on the number of pulses. In a few cases, the two classes of mechanisms are even related to each other. Eventually, we will show the implications that incubation has on real-world laser machining.

item.title: First Steps towards Machine Learning for Prediction and Pre-Correction in Direct Laser Writing
item.description: arXiv:2511.23306v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Additive manufacturing using 2-Photon Polymerization (2PP, aka direct laser writing DLW) enables the fabrication of almost arbitrary complex 3D structures from the meso to the submicron scale. However, deviations between the anticipated target structure and the actual print often occur due to physico-chemical processes, limiting the accuracy and reliability of this technology. To minimize these deviations, we hereby present our latest research in developing different neural networks, targeting the above-mentioned aspect. Our networks are trained on several experimental as well as theoretical datasets and show good results in predicting fabrication deviations and (pre-) correcting 2.5D micro-structures. Hence, we demonstrate, that besides conventional iterative correction methods, neural networks are a promising alternative to significantly improving the output quality in DLW. Furthermore, there are no fundamental limitations to transferring this machine learning approach to other 3D printing technologies, as they all face the same challenge in terms of fidelity. To our point of view, the use of neural networks has the potential to enhance the capabilities of this technology, enabling the creation of complex structures with increased accuracy and precision in the near future.
item.dc:creator: Sven Enns, Julian Hering-Stratemeier, Georg von Freymann

item.title: Optomechanical Limit on Intracavity Intensities from Bulk Mirror Vibrations
item.description: arXiv:2602.23476v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Ultrahigh continuous-wave intensities (>300 GW/cm$^2$) in high-numerical-aperture optical cavities enable applications from phase-contrast electron microscopy to ultradeep dipole traps for molecules. However, the intensity can be limited by the optomechanical parametric instability (PI), where mirror vibrations scatter light from one cavity mode into another. We observe parametric instability in a tabletop Fabry-P\'erot cavity, show that the mechanical modes are MHz-frequency bulk acoustic modes inside the mirrors, and measure their $Q$ factor. By using low-$Q$ mirrors, we achieve >500 GW/cm$^2$ intensities in an open, free-space cavity.
item.dc:creator: L. Maisenbacher, A. Singh, I. M. Pope, H. M\"uller

item.title: Independent amplitude and phase modulation using two sequential regions of one phase-only SLM
item.description: arXiv:2606.07821v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Liquid-crystal spatial light modulators (SLMs) are widely used for programmable wavefront control but are typically operated as phase-only devices, limiting applications that require independent amplitude and phase shaping. Here we demonstrate full complex-field modulation using a single phase-only SLM by implementing two sequential modulation planes on different regions of the same device. The phase retardance introduced by the first SLM region is converted into amplitude modulation by a polarizer placed in the beam path, while the second region compensates the associated phase offset and imposes the required phase distribution. The field from the first region is imaged onto the second, enabling complex-field synthesis without a second modulator. We validate the approach by generating Bessel--Gaussian beams, helical-phase fields, and arbitrary focal-plane intensity patterns. This single-SLM platform provides a compact route to programmable complex wavefront engineering for structured illumination, holography, and electron--light interaction experiments.
item.dc:creator: Marius Constantin Chirita Mihaila, Mikul\'a\v{s} Fiala, Martin Koz\'ak

item.title: Discrete phase symmetry of stationary states in bichromatically pumped Kerr microresonators
item.description: arXiv:2606.12749v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Bichromatically pumped Kerr microresonators can exhibit phase multistability due to four-wave mixing between the pump modes and the generated modes. Here, we analyze the symmetry structure of stationary solutions within the coupled-mode description of these systems. We show that the two-pump coupled-mode equations belong to a broader class of models with equally spaced driven modes and mode-dependent nonlinear coupling coefficients, losses, and detunings. In this generalized setting, each stationary solution generates a finite family of stationary solutions under a discrete phase transformation. For each nonzero modal amplitude, the number of distinct phase values within a symmetry orbit is determined solely by the mode index and the pump-mode spacing. We show that the phase-counting rule also applies to modes outside the interval between the two pumps, where it reproduces the symmetry observed within that interval. In addition, the same phase-multistability mechanism can arise in configurations with multiple pump modes, provided that adjacent pumps are separated by the same number of resonator modes.

item.title: Transverse Modulation of Continuous Electron Beams by a Structured Optical Cavity
item.description: arXiv:2606.16958v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Compact aberration correction at large semi-angles remains a central challenge in electron microscopy. Here we propose a phase plate for continuous electron beams based on the ponderomotive interaction with an intracavity standing wave in a near-concentric Fabry--P\'erot resonator. For electrons propagating along the cavity axis, a standing-wave with Laguerre-Gaussian mode of topological charge $l=1$ imprints an annular phase shift that is opposite in sign to the third-order spherical aberration of a conventional electron lens. For a \(5~\mathrm{keV}\) beam with a convergence semi-angle of \(25~\mathrm{mrad}\), we fully compensate the third-order spherical aberration of an objective lens with \(C_\mathrm{s}=1~\mathrm{mm}\), yielding the transverse width of the corrected probe in the focus of \(\sigma_\mathrm{p}=1.4~\mathrm{\AA}\). The accessible transverse electron phases are set by the supported resonator modal basis and its coherent superpositions.

item.title: Demonstration of Flying-Focus-Enhanced Relativistic Thomson Scattering
item.description: arXiv:2607.15805v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We report the experimental demonstration of a spatiotemporally engineered "flying-focus" laser pulse for enhanced X-ray generation via relativistic Thomson scattering. By combining longitudinal chromatic aberration, angular dispersion, and group delay dispersion, we create a relativistically intense laser pulse whose focal point propagates with an independently tunable velocity vector, enabling control of both its speed and propagation angle. Precise tuning of the focal-point trajectory is used to match the motion of a near-counterpropagating ultrarelativistic electron bunch generated by a laser wakefield accelerator. This spatiotemporal velocity matching extends the interaction length while mitigating nonlinear scattering effects, resulting in an enhanced X-ray yield. Simulations indicate that this approach can increase the spectral density and brightness of Thomson-scattered X-ray beams by orders of magnitude relative to equivalent focusing without spatiotemporal control. The technique provides a new degree of freedom for high-intensity laser-matter interactions, allowing dynamic intensity structures with programmable two-dimensional motion and opening a route to enhanced laser-particle interactions and next-generation ultrabright radiation sources.

item.title: Cavity optomechanics with a suspended resonant mirror
item.description: arXiv:2608.02488v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We investigate optomechanical effects in cavities consisting of a plane-plane arrangement of a broadband reflectivity mirror and an ultrathin, suspended resonant mirror possessing a high-Q internal optical resonance. We first investigate dispersive and photothermal optomechanics in such cavities on the basis of a generic analytical model as well as finite element method simulations of realistic structures. We then report on experimental optical spring measurements using a suspended silicon nitride membrane patterned with a subwavelength grating. The observed optical spring variations match those expected from the theoretical model, but with a magnitude several hundreds times larger than expected from the dispersive optomechanical coupling only, thus suggesting strong photothermal optomechanical coupling.

item.title: Multiphysics simulation of all-optical switching and sequential magneto-optic readout in an integrated Si$_3$N$_4$/GdFeCo waveguide
item.description: arXiv:2608.22969v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Femtosecond pulses guided in a silicon nitride waveguide have recently switched a Co/Gd magnetic element patterned on top of it, a step towards magnetic memory built into photonic circuits. The guided mode heats such an element non-uniformly, and, to our knowledge, no calculation has yet followed the written state from this heating to an optical readout. Here we model both steps for an 8 nm GdFeCo film inserted across a Si$_3$N$_4$ waveguide. A three-dimensional finite-difference time-domain calculation gives the absorbed pump energy. This energy drives a four-temperature model and calibrated stochastic Landau-Lifshitz-Bloch dynamics, and a later probe pulse reads the recovered state. At the reference fluence, a single pump pulse reverses 86% of the film from either saturated state, and this fraction changes little over a 2.4-fold range of incident fluence. The unswitched cells lie where the absorbed fluence stays below the single-cell threshold, and a threshold rule applied to the absorption map reproduces the full calculation. When the film starts from zero magnetization, thermal noise sets the direction of each recovered local moment at random. Between the saturated and random states, the probe energy fractions change by at most 0.02. The magnetic Faraday and Kerr rotations are far more sensitive and become about 12 and 130 times smaller, respectively, in the random state than in a saturated film. The reflected signal also contains a magnetization-independent geometric background, which can be removed by subtracting a reference signal. The model therefore predicts that a guided probe can distinguish the written states through its polarization. It assumes a homogeneous film and omits heat flow and exchange between neighbouring cells.

item.title: SHAPE: a sparse Hamiltonian approach for prescribing eigenstates in metamaterials
item.description: arXiv:2610.37248v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Metamaterials, which store, guide and emit waves through their eigenstates, have enabled the development of devices with diverse functionalities. Yet the spatial profiles of conventional metamaterials' eigenstates are typically determined by their pre-determined structures (Hamiltonians). Here we develop SHAPE, a sparse Hamiltonian approach that enables the realization of prescribed, spectrally isolated eigenstates in physically realizable metamaterials. The resulting Hamiltonian geometries obey a boundary law, with the required nonlocality determined solely by single-contact boundary sites ($|E_{\mathrm{LR}}| = |\partial\Omega|$), independent of the state interior or lattice size. The Hamiltonians are further spectrally reshaped to open a protective gap around the target eigenstate. We validate our approach in discrete lattices and acoustic metamaterials. We provide a database of over 100 target states and a customizable design program, demonstrating the generality and extensibility of our method. Although demonstrated in acoustics, the principle can be applied to thermal, electrical-circuit and photonic metamaterials.
item.dc:creator: Yutao Chen, Tao Xiao, Jing Li, Aodong Li, Biye Xie

item.title: Nonperturbative theory of thin-vapor-layer linear optical properties: towards the optimal design of alkali-metal vapor nanocells
item.description: arXiv:2611.00400v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Hot alkali-metal vapors confined inside nanometer-thick spectroscopic cells are highly suitable media for miniature and cheap frequency standards, magnetometers and atomic sensors. Yet their linear optical properties at low to moderate atomic densities are not fully understood. The main reason is the complex, strongly nonlocal optical response of such systems to resonant radiation, which arises from the free motion of atoms and their collisions with the walls. To date, calculations of reflection and transmission spectra of these cells have been restricted to perturbation theory in the atomic density for the case of quenching atom-wall collisions, which has substantially limited their practical use. Here we introduce a rigorous numerical approach for computing thin-vapor-layer spectra that accurately accounts for the nonlocal optical response at arbitrary optical density and layer thickness. Our model predicts a density-dependent blue shift of the resonance that is absent in the first-order perturbative description. We show that its values are comparable to the homogeneous width of an atomic transition and, therefore, too large to be neglected in most cases. Next, inspired by recent experiments, we explore a wide range of vapor layer thicknesses and study how the reflectivity and its derivative with respect to the laser detuning depend on the layer thickness. We obtain an approximate expression for the thickness maximising the first derivative of the reflectivity that agrees closely with the rigorous numerical model and reduces to the first-order analytical result showing the optima at $l=\lambda/3+n\lambda$ and $l=2\lambda/3+n\lambda$, where $n$ is a non-negative integer. These results provide a practical design tool for nanometer-thick spectroscopic cells in various applications and a starting point for further development of the theory.
item.dc:creator: Andrei V. Ermolaev, Tigran A. Vartanyan

item.title: Neuromorphic Camera for Multi-Target Pointing Acquisition and Tracking in Free Space Optical Communication
item.description: arXiv:2611.05503v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Pointing, Acquisition, and Tracking (PAT) in Free-Space Optical Communication (FSOC) applications must achieve both low jitter and a large Field of View (FoV) to support beacon acquisition and multi-target tracking. While conventional frame-based sensors provide the necessary angular coverage, their performance is limited by latency, available frame-rate, and motion blur. This work explores and demonstrates the application of an event-based vision sensor for PAT tasks in FSOC. The system employs a neuromorphic sensor that asynchronously records brightness changes (events) with microsecond-level temporal resolution. The main contribution of this paper is a comparative analysis of event-based tracking algorithms for the simultaneous acquisition and tracking of multiple optical beacons that operate directly on this asynchronous stream. The performance of these strategies is validated on an experimental dataset representing realistic operational conditions for dynamic High-Altitude Platform (HAP) and Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) networks. The analysis compares key metrics, such as tracking accuracy and processing latency, under various signal-to-background conditions.

item.title: Non-Equilibrium Ising-Bloch Transition in Polarization Cavity Solitons
item.description: arXiv:2611.12626v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Polarization cavity solitons in coherently driven Kerr resonators undergo a sequence of dynamical bifurcations as the cavity detuning is increased. Here we show that a stationary localized state containing an Ising wall first becomes a fixed breather and then develops finite chirality and drift motion through a spontaneous non-equilibrium Ising-Bloch transition. Stability analyses identify the modes responsible for the breathing and the motion, revealing controllable dynamics of polarization cavity solitons.

item.title: Tidal potential measured with distant optical clocks
item.description: arXiv:2611.14293v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Fibre-linked optical clocks sense tidal changes of the gravitational potential, but separating overlapping tidal components and quantifying their precision remain challenging. Using strontium and ytterbium clocks 692 km apart, we measure over 353 days a response of 0.95 (0.11) to the combined solid-Earth and ocean-loading tide and 1.01 (0.13) for the lunar semidiurnal group, and separate the lunar and solar-frequency semidiurnal contributions. A signal-to-noise model based on the actual sampling accounts for the lunar precision and guides future clock-network observations.

item.title: Probing tensor monopoles and gerbe invariants in three-dimensional topological matter
item.description: arXiv:2507.22116v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We show that momentum-space tensor monopoles corresponding to nontrivial vector bundle generalizations, known as bundle gerbes, can be realized in bands of three-dimensional topological matter with nontrivial Hopf invariants. We provide a universal construction of tensor Berry connections in these topological phases, demonstrating how obstructions therein lead to $\mathbb{Z}$-quantized bulk magnetoelectric and nonlinear optical phenomena in the presence of spacetime inversion ($\mathcal{PT}$) symmetry. We then pinpoint that these quantum effects are supported by intraband and interband torsion leading to nontrivial Dixmier-Douady classes in most known Hopf phases and in more general topological insulators realizing gerbe invariants falling beyond the tenfold classification of topological phases of matter. We furthermore provide an interacting generalization upon introducing many-body gerbe invariants by employing twisted boundary conditions. This opens an avenue to study gerbe invariants realized through higher-dimensional charge fractionalizations that can be electromagnetically probed.
item.dc:creator: Wojciech J. Jankowski, Robert-Jan Slager, Giandomenico Palumbo

item.title: Giant spontaneous Kerr effect and its self-doping dependence in altermagnetic MnTe
item.description: arXiv:2604.21021v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Altermagnetism, a third class of collinear magnetism with spin-split bands and vanishing net magnetization, has emerged in hexagonal {\alpha}-MnTe, a promising platform for ultrafast, stray-field-free spintronics. Whether MnTe's macroscopic symmetry-breaking signatures reflect ideal altermagnetic order or are activated by defects remains open. Here we report giant spontaneous Kerr rotations of up to 1500 rad in {\alpha}-MnTe single crystals at the telecommunication wavelength of 1550 nm, onsetting precisely at the N\'eel temperature TN = 307 K. The signal appears in disjoint macroscopic patches whose amplitude tracks the sample conductivity, and a hole-conducting {\alpha}-MnTe film reproduces this response together with an anomalous Hall effect. Within a single crystal, Kerr-active regions are optically distinct from their Kerr-silent surroundings in co-registered reflection maps. These observations indicate that carrier self-doping, rather than ideal altermagnetic order alone, governs the giant magneto-optical response, and establish telecom-wavelength Kerr imaging as a practical readout for altermagnetic spintronics.

item.title: Broadband High-Level Squeezed Light using Waveguide Optical Parametric Amplifiers with External Dispersion Compensation
item.description: arXiv:2606.17422v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We demonstrate broadband phase-sensitive amplification (PSA) measurement of squeezed light generated by a waveguide optical parametric amplifier (OPA) with external dispersion compensation. In broadband systems, group velocity dispersion (GVD) induces a frequency-dependent rotation of the squeezing axis, which limits the observable bandwidth in PSA measurements. While dispersion compensation between two OPAs has been demonstrated previously, we show that the quantity to be compensated is not the material group-delay dispersion $D$ itself but a gain-dependent effective value $D\tanh r/(2r)$, where $r$ is the squeezing parameter, and realize the compensation with free-space fused-silica plates whose insertion loss is $0.4\%$. As a result, we observe a maximum squeezing of $5.9\pm0.2$~dB near the carrier frequency and more than 5~dB of squeezing up to a frequency offset of $5.9\pm0.1$ THz from the carrier. Furthermore, squeezing below the shot-noise level is confirmed up to a frequency offset of $6.9\pm0.1$ THz from the carrier, corresponding to the accessible phase-matching bandwidth of the waveguide OPA. Our results establish a practical method for broadband characterization of squeezed light and provide a key step toward ultrafast continuous-variable quantum information processing.

item.title: Absolute displacement calibration of a levitated nanoparticle with real-time heterodyne demodulation
item.description: arXiv:2607.09912v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We report a heterodyne scheme for the position readout of an optomechanical system, in particular an optically levitated nanoparticle, based on digital in-phase and quadrature demodulation on a field-programmable gate array. Compared to the standard homodyne approach, it offers three key advantages: it requires no phase lock, it produces a signal linearly proportional to the particle displacement, and its calibration is immune to drifts in the optical power of the local oscillator and of the scattered field. Combined with a vectorial model of the focal field, it measures the displacement in length units without free parameters. Through simultaneous homodyne and heterodyne measurements on the same trapped particle we demonstrate these advantages: the heterodyne follows a driven particle linearly up to amplitudes at which the homodyne response folds back, and calibrates the homodyne, whose standard thermometric calibration we find biased by 33 %. Inverting equipartition, the calibrated readout measures the mass of the particle with an uncertainty below 1 %, after removing a bias of up to 20 % caused by absorption heating at 1550 nm. The method can be used in any optomechanical system based on phase readout.

item.title: Reading Why: Born-Measured Attention with Exact Word Evidence on Light and Qubits
item.description: arXiv:2611.05355v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: When a language model answers, we can usually only estimate why. We build a transformer in which every nonlinearity is a quadratic detection - an interference, a balanced reading or a camera - and the output is a Born probability: attention |<q|k>|^2, the form of the Born rule, normalised per row, a measured product for the feed-forward nonlinearity, and a Born readout; between detections, classical control rescales and re-encodes. With its denominators held at the input, each class probability is a polynomial in the word amplitudes, so its integrated-gradient evidence is computed by a finite quadrature with no quadrature error: the words' contributions sum to the class probability above its no-information share to 10^-13. On e-SNLI natural language inference it reaches 77.45 +- 0.91 % accuracy, level with a same-size softmax transformer (76.62 +- 0.36 %) and an order-free bag of embeddings (77.79 %). Exactness buys the sum, not the best ranking. Deleting the word its evidence ranks first changes the answer in 44 % of pairs, of the 53 % some deletion changes, against 31-32 % for the softmax model's integrated gradients; the model's own gradient x input does as well (43 %), as does a bag of embeddings' (43 %, seed 0), and leave-one-out does better. Holding the denominators helps the low end: the five words ranked last change the answer in 1 %, against 6 % free. The same weights compile exactly to simulated optoelectronics, and their attention to qubits. On ibm_kingston, reading only the attention, the device gave the model's answers in all three Hadamard-test runs (the two shortest pairs and one without its deciding word) and both compute-uncompute runs (one circuit per overlap); uniform attention answers otherwise on two of the three inputs. With the device's row sums the evidence correlated with the exact one at 0.997 and 0.962 by Hadamard tests; with compute-uncompute, 0.971 and 0.48.
